appraisal_events.evidence: « elle sut me parler très bien des raffinements d’Elstir » ; « Les robes de Mme Elstir passaient inaperçues aux yeux de quelqu’un qui n’avait pas le goût sûr et sobre des choses de la toilette. Il me faisait défaut. » ; « en réalité, bien que cela ne se vît guère encore, elle était très intelligente et dans les choses qu’elle disait, la bêtise n’était pas sienne, mais celle de son milieu et de son âge »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly revalues Albertine upward: she out-sees him on dress and painting, corrects his misreading of Mme Elstir's simplicity, and he certifies her real intelligence, assigning her apparent silliness to her milieu rather than to herself. Her sweeping disparagement of the d'Ambresac girls (« les petites oies blanches ») is staged within this same movement as evidence of a discriminating, authoritative voice, not as a separate appraisal act.

appraisal_events.evidence: Elstir reveals the picnic Andrée had accepted, exposing her excuse about her sick mother as a lie ; « je n’aurais pas dû continuer à fréquenter une personne qui en était capable. Car ce que les gens ont fait, ils le recommencent indéfiniment. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Andrée's fabricated excuse is caught out through Elstir, and the narrator converts the trivial lie into an endorsed general condemnation of her character. Her coldness toward the narrator and the closing report that she is hated by, and denounces, the other girl reinforce the same downward local movement.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator explicitly credits her with intelligence, sure taste, and disinterested delicacy, exempting her from the stupidity of her milieu.
She holds the floor throughout, laughs at and corrects the narrator's judgment of Mme Elstir's dress, and rules on who is chic and who is ridiculous while he concedes his own deficiency.

The same passage elevates Elstir by association and directly: his taste is said to be supreme, his patiently pursued objects are revealed as marvels, and he is credited with a happy formative influence on Albertine.
Her exposed lie leads the narrator to a settled adverse judgment of her as someone whose falsehood will recur.

ambiguities: In the closing exchange, « J’ai supporté longtemps sa terrible fausseté, me dit-elle » could momentarily be read as the golden-haired girl denouncing Andrée; the strongest reading makes Andrée the speaker, since the following sentence says the gossip « qu’avait fait cette jeune fille » could harm Andrée. That denunciation is annotated only as reinforcing E2's atmosphere, not as its own event, because its target is an unnamed girl absent from the reference sheet.

Albertine's own praise of Andrée (« Andrée au moins est remarquablement intelligente ») cuts locally against the narrator's condemnation of her; the narrator's explicitly endorsed judgment on the lie is treated as dominant, and the narrator's separate chagrin at Saint-Loup's concealed engagement is left unrecorded under the two-event cap.
